titre: Miners Oppose the Law That Banishes Women from Underground Work
accroche: In 1842, British workers themselves challenge the bill meant to forbid women and children from working underground.
contenu_vulgarise:
Silkstone, Yorkshire, July 4, 1838. Violent storms make a stream overflow into the ventilation drift of the Huskar colliery: twenty-six children drown, eleven girls aged eight to sixteen and fifteen boys aged nine to twelve. The news reaches Queen Victoria, who orders an inquiry. The MP Anthony Ashley-Cooper, then known by the title Lord Ashley, chairs the royal commission charged with examining the employment of children in mines. Published in May 1842, its report, accompanied by illustrations, mostly by the artist Margaret Gillies, and by testimony gathered from the miners, reveals that children of five or six work as trappers, opening and closing the ventilation doors, before becoming hurriers, dragging coal carts on all fours, and that women work underground, bare to the waist because of the heat, alongside men.

## A Total Ban, an Age Threshold

The bill Lord Ashley defends in the Commons does not merely limit hours: it flatly forbids the employment of any woman or girl, whatever her age, underground in mines and collieries, and sets ten as the minimum age for underground employment of boys. On July 5, 1842, at the third reading in the Commons, the text clears a decisive step. It will still have to wait nearly a year, however: the act, known as the Mines and Collieries Act, receives royal assent only on June 9, 1843, while the date given to it, 1842, remains that of the report and the initial vote.

## A Law Voted Against the Wishes of Those It Protects

That July 5, in the Commons, the debate takes an unexpected turn. The MP Ainsworth presents fifteen or sixteen petitions from workers around Bradford, opposed to the text. He reports the case of a Lancashire operator employing one hundred twenty boys, sixty of them under thirteen and thirty-two under nine, who, if the law passed as it stood, would lose all means of subsistence. In Scotland, he adds, at least forty widows depend entirely on their children's work. What the law takes from children and women are jobs that, however harsh, kept families alive with no other income: opposition to the text thus does not come only from mine owners.

Enforcement then runs into a more prosaic obstacle: a single inspector is appointed for the entire United Kingdom. In 1850, the administration still has to note that two hundred women and girls are working in the collieries of South Wales. A law can thus gather a vote, a resounding commission of inquiry, and illustrations that shock public opinion, and remain largely a dead letter as long as no one is charged with enforcing it, which is hardly a problem unique to the nineteenth century.

citation.texte: To the exclusion of women from collieries he had not the slightest objection; but he thought that just now their exclusion would increase the distress which already prevailed amongst the poor and labouring population of the country.
citation.auteur: Mr. Ainsworth, MP in the Commons
citation.source: Commons debate on the Mines and Collieries Bill, July 5, 1842, Hansard, HC Deb vol. 64, cc999-1009

carte.punch: Workers themselves protested against the law meant to protect them
carte.idee: In 1842, a British commission reveals that five-year-old children work underground in mines and that women toil there bare to the waist. The bill meant to banish them is nonetheless fought by workers' petitions, which fear the loss of the only income of entire families.

quiz.question: Why do workers' petitions oppose, in July 1842, the bill meant to forbid women from working underground in British mines?
choix: Because they judge the measure insufficient and also demand a ban on men's work
Because they fear that excluding women and children would deprive whole families of their only income
Because they consider that mine safety has already improved enough since the Huskar disaster
Because they ask that the measure also apply to textile mills, not only to mines
quiz.explication: The MP Ainsworth reports to the Commons petitions from Yorkshire workers and cites the example of a Lancashire operator employing one hundred twenty boys, many under thirteen, who would lose all means of subsistence if the law passed as it stood.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What triggers the royal commission chaired by Lord Ashley?
choix: A union report denouncing wages that are too low in the collieries
The drowning of twenty-six children in the Huskar colliery in 1838, during a storm
A general strike of Yorkshire miners demanding a minimum-age law
A press article about working conditions in Scottish mines
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The drowning of twenty-six children at Huskar in 1838, when storms made the ventilation drift overflow, provokes a royal inquiry whose 1842 report underpins the bill.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What exactly does the report published in May 1842 reveal about child labor?
choix: That children of five or six work as trappers, before becoming hurriers
That most children employed in mines are over fourteen
That child labor is already banned in most British collieries
That women are employed only in surface mines, never underground
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 1842 report describes children of five or six employed as trappers, before becoming hurriers, dragging coal carts on all fours.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does the law remain largely unenforced after its adoption?
choix: Because it provides no penalty for violations found
Because it is repealed as early as 1845 under pressure from mine owners
Because a single inspector is appointed to oversee its enforcement across the whole United Kingdom
Because royal assent is never granted to the text voted in 1842
quiz_supplementaire.explication: A single inspector is appointed for the whole United Kingdom, so that in 1850 about two hundred women and girls are still working in the collieries of South Wales.
